words: cite; evidence; explicit; inference; infer; quotation; support
notes: Citing textual evidence to back both what a text says outright and what a reader infers from it, in stories, poems and literary nonfiction: the student states a point, quotes or points to the line, and says how the line supports it (a two-part answer: point, then quoted line with its page or paragraph). Grade 5 asked students to quote accurately; grade 6 asks them to cite evidence in support of their own analysis, so the quote now serves a claim the student makes. One piece of well-chosen evidence per point is the grade 6 bar (several pieces is grade 7). Practised on every anchor of the year, from short original stories and poems to recent public-domain government nonfiction, all in the lower part of the grades 6 to 8 band with support. RL.6.1 and RI.6.1 share the row because the skill is the same in both kinds of text; RI.6.1 adds citing from charts, captions and headings.

words: theme; central idea; detail; convey; summary; opinion; objective
notes: Determining a theme of a story, poem or drama and how particular details convey it, then writing a summary that keeps the student's opinions and judgments out. Grade 5 asked for a theme drawn from how characters respond to challenges, and a summary; grade 6 adds how the theme is conveyed through particular details and asks the summary to be distinct from personal opinion (no 'I liked', no judging the character). A theme is a statement about life, not a one-word topic ('loss' is a topic; 'people carry grief differently and need not hide it' is a theme). Practised on short original stories and narrative poems of 800 to 2,500 words and on the year's long text. Limit: one theme traced through its details; tracing a theme's development across a whole text is grade 7.

words: plot; episode; conflict; rising action; climax; resolution; respond; change
notes: Describing how a story's or drama's plot unfolds in a series of episodes and how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution. Grade 5 compared characters, settings or events; grade 6 follows one plot episode by episode and tracks a character's response or change at each step (a character-change line drawn under the plot map). Practised on original realistic and adventure fiction about the age group (school, family, a first job, a team) of 1,500 to 4,000 words, and on chapters of the year's long text. Limit: describing what unfolds; analysing how story elements act on each other (setting shaping plot) is grade 7, and how a line of dialogue propels action is grade 8.

words: figurative; literal; connotation; denotation; tone; personification; word choice
notes: Working out what words and phrases mean as used in a story or poem, including figurative and connotative meanings, and analysing how one word choice shapes meaning and tone (why 'shuffled' and not 'walked'). Grade 5 asked for figurative meaning (simile and metaphor); grade 6 adds connotation and the impact of a word choice on tone. L.6.5 sits here because its texts practise it: L.6.5a interpreting personification and other figures in context, L.6.5c ranking words with similar denotations by connotation (stingy, thrifty, economical). L.6.5b, word relationships, is owned by e6-word-strategies. Practised on short original poems (10 to 40 lines) and descriptive passages of the year's stories, reread for word choice after a first read for meaning. Limit: tone is named and supported from words; sound devices (rhyme, alliteration) are grade 7.

words: structure; stanza; scene; chapter; contribute; setting; flashback
notes: Analysing how one sentence, chapter, scene or stanza fits into the whole text and contributes to the theme, setting or plot (why the story opens in the hospital waiting room; what the last stanza turns). Grade 5 explained how a series of chapters, scenes or stanzas fits together; grade 6 narrows to one part and asks what it does for the whole. Practised on short original stories, poems with three or more stanzas, a short original one-act play, and chapters of the long text. Limit: the part's job inside one text; how a form (sonnet, soliloquy) makes meaning is grade 7, and comparing the structures of two texts is grade 8.

words: narrator; speaker; point of view; first person; third person; perspective; reliable
notes: Explaining how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker: what the narrator notices, knows, misses and feels, and the words and details that build that view. Introduces the point-of-view model, a new shared name (none of the listed models fits): a chart of who tells, what they know, what they think, and what the reader comes to know. Grade 5 described how a narrator's point of view influences how events are described; grade 6 asks how the author builds that view. Practised on original first-person stories and dramatic monologue poems where the narrator is close to the reader's age. Limit: one narrator or speaker; contrasting the views of several characters is grade 7 and the gap between characters and reader (dramatic irony) is grade 8.

words: audio; version; perceive; imagine; performance; recording
notes: Comparing and contrasting the experience of reading a story, drama or poem with listening to or watching an audio, video or live version, including what readers picture when reading against what they perceive when they listen or watch. Grade 5 analysed how visual and multimedia elements add to a text's meaning; grade 6 sets the reading experience beside a performance of the same text. Practised on an original poem with a recorded reading, and a scene of the year's original play read first and then performed by the class or played from a recording made for the course. Limit: the student's own experience, described with evidence from both; naming techniques unique to each medium is grade 7 and judging a director's choices is grade 8. Teacher note: any recording used is made for the course or in the public domain.

words: genre; form; compare; contrast; approach; historical fiction; fantasy
notes: Comparing and contrasting texts in different forms or genres (a story and a poem; a historical story and a fantasy) on how each approaches a similar theme or topic. Grade 5 compared stories in the same genre; grade 6 crosses genres and asks how the form shapes the approach. Practised on a paired set inside one unit topic, for example an original story and an original poem about moving to a new place, or a short historical story and a fantasy tale on keeping a promise; each piece 500 to 2,500 words. The written comparison is practised with e6-text-response-writing (W.6.9a names this standard). Limit: two texts on one theme; a fictional portrayal against a historical account is grade 7.

words: stamina; reread; complex; long text; independent reading; log
notes: Reading and understanding literature (stories, dramas, poems) and literary nonfiction in the grades 6 to 8 complexity band by the end of the year, with support as needed at the high end. Grade 5 asked for the high end of the grades 4 to 5 band independently; grade 6 moves into the new band, so support returns at its upper end. The 2012 supplement's 6 to 8 band (925 to 1185 on its first scale) is the measure; a working split, ours and not from the source, places most grade 6 anchors in the lower half with a few at the top with support. Covers the year's volume: one long text read whole (an original novella or a recent public-domain government nonfiction book), shorter anchors in every unit, independent reading with a log and conferences. RL.6.10 and RI.6.10 share the row because both are the same staircase in the two kinds of text; the year's anchors aim at about 55 percent informational. No standard below this is reached without this row's texts.

words: central idea; supporting detail; convey; summary; objective; paraphrase
notes: Determining a central idea of an informational text and how particular details convey it, and summarising the text without personal opinions. Grade 5 asked for two or more main ideas and how key details support them; grade 6 shifts to a central idea conveyed through details and adds the opinion-free summary (the same summary demand as RL.6.2, on information). Practised on recent public-domain government articles and original feature articles of 600 to 1,500 words, on topics the unit's set builds (for example how a city prepares for floods). Limit: one central idea per text; two or more developed across a text is grade 7.

words: introduce; illustrate; elaborate; anecdote; example; key individual
notes: Analysing in detail how a key individual, event or idea is introduced, illustrated and elaborated in a text, through examples and anecdotes (how a profile of a young inventor opens with one failed test, then gives the numbers, then a quote). Grade 5 explained relationships between individuals, events or ideas; grade 6 follows one of them through the text's moves. Practised on literary nonfiction: profiles, short memoir excerpts and feature articles of 800 to 2,000 words, original or recent public-domain. Limit: one individual, event or idea; interactions among several is grade 7, and connections and distinctions drawn by analogy or category is grade 8.

words: technical; domain-specific; general academic; connotation; define; glossary
notes: Determining the meaning of words and phrases in informational text, including figurative, connotative and technical meanings, and acquiring the unit's general academic and domain words (L.6.6 sits here: the unit word list is drawn from these texts, met before, during and after reading and returned to in later units). Grade 5 asked for general academic and domain words of a grade 5 topic; grade 6 adds figurative and connotative meanings in nonfiction and the habit of gathering word knowledge when a word matters. Practised on the unit's informational anchors, chiefly science and history articles. Limit: meaning in context; analysing the impact of a word choice on tone in nonfiction is grade 7.

words: structure; section; paragraph; heading; chronology; cause and effect; problem and solution
notes: Analysing how a sentence, paragraph, chapter or section fits into the overall structure of a text and adds to the development of its ideas (why the article puts the history section before the solutions). Grade 5 compared the overall structures of two texts; grade 6 looks at the job one part does inside one text. Practised on informational articles with headings and on chapters of a longer nonfiction work, 800 to 2,500 words. Limit: one part in one text; how the major sections build the whole is grade 7, and the role of each sentence in one paragraph is grade 8.

words: author's purpose; point of view; persuade; inform; audience; convey
notes: Determining an author's point of view or purpose in an informational text and explaining how the text conveys it (word choice, what is included and left out, the examples chosen). Introduces the rhetorical-situation model here (author, audience, purpose, occasion), used again in this grade's writing and speaking rows. Grade 5 analysed several accounts of one event and the points of view they represent; grade 6 asks how one author's point of view or purpose shows in the text. Practised on short opinion pieces, public service notices and agency explainers (recent public-domain) and original articles, 400 to 1,500 words. Limit: one author's view; how an author sets that view against others is grade 7.

words: graph; chart; map; table; integrate; data; format
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.4 (reading dot plots and histograms in a text)
notes: Integrating information given in charts, graphs, maps, photographs and numbers with the words of a text to build one understanding of a topic, and explaining how a piece of media information adds to the topic (SL.6.2 adds the same work on information heard or seen: a short recorded explainer, a narrated map). Grade 5 drew on several sources to locate an answer quickly; grade 6 asks the reader to join formats into one coherent picture. Practised on government reports and explainers with a data display (weather, population, a park's visitor numbers) and on one short recorded clip per unit. Limit: integrating formats; evaluating which medium serves a topic best is grade 8.

words: argument; claim; reason; evidence; supported; unsupported
notes: Tracing and evaluating the argument and specific claims in a text, sorting claims backed by reasons and evidence from claims that are not. Introduces the argument-map model (claim at the top, reasons under it, evidence under each reason, and a mark on any claim left bare). SL.6.3 sits here: the same delineation on a speaker's argument in a recorded or live talk. Grade 5 explained how an author uses reasons and evidence to support points; grade 6 adds the judgment of which claims are supported. Practised on short arguments: editorials written for the course, a school board speech, a public comment letter, 300 to 1,000 words. Limit: supported or not; whether reasoning is sound and evidence sufficient is grade 7, and spotting irrelevant evidence is grade 8.

words: memoir; biography; account; presentation; compare; contrast
notes: Comparing and contrasting one author's presentation of events with another's, for example a memoir by a person and a biography about the same person. Grade 5 integrated information from several texts on one topic; grade 6 asks how two authors present the same events differently (what each includes, the order, the voice). Practised on a paired set: an original first-person account and an original or public-domain profile of the same person or event, each 600 to 2,000 words. Limit: describing the difference in presentation; analysing how authors shape key information by choosing different evidence is grade 7.

words: argument; claim; reason; evidence; credible; formal style; conclusion
notes: Writing arguments that support a claim with clear reasons and relevant evidence: introduce the claim and organise the reasons and evidence clearly (W.6.1a), use credible sources (b), link claim and reasons with words and clauses (c), keep a formal style (d), and end with a conclusion that follows (e). Grade 5 wrote opinion pieces; grade 6 is the first year of argument proper, with evidence from sources and formal style. Two pieces a year, one through the full process, drawing on the unit's texts. Limit: one claim with its reasons; acknowledging opposing claims is grade 7. The year's writing is about 35 percent argument.

words: topic; definition; classification; compare; cause; effect; transition; precise
cross_subject: science:s6-hazard-forecast (an explanation of a natural hazard with a chart)
notes: Writing informative and explanatory texts: introduce a topic and organise it by definition, classification, comparison and contrast, or cause and effect, with headings and a chart where they help (W.6.2a); develop it with facts, definitions, details and quotations (b); use transitions (c), precise and domain words (d), formal style (e) and a conclusion that follows (f). Grade 5 grouped related information logically; grade 6 names the organising strategies and adds formal style. Two to three pieces a year drawing on the unit's informational texts, at least one through the full process. Limit: transitions that clarify; transitions that create cohesion and a preview of what follows are grade 7.

words: narrator; sequence; dialogue; pacing; description; sensory; transition
notes: Writing real or imagined narratives: orient the reader and introduce a narrator and characters with an event sequence that unfolds naturally (W.6.3a), use dialogue, pacing and description (b), signal shifts in time and setting (c), use precise and sensory language (d), and end with a conclusion that follows (e). Grade 5 used the same techniques with less control of time shifts; grade 6 adds pacing and transitions that signal a shift in time frame or setting. Model texts are the unit's anchor stories; two pieces a year, one through the full process. Limit: the narrator is introduced; establishing a point of view on purpose is grade 7.

words: task; purpose; audience; coherent; publish; keyboard; collaborate
notes: Producing clear, coherent writing whose development, organisation and style fit the task, purpose and audience (W.6.4), and using technology to produce, publish and collaborate, with enough keyboarding to type three pages in one sitting (W.6.6). Grade 5 asked for two pages in one sitting; grade 6 raises it to three and adds online collaboration. The rhetorical-situation model is the planning check before each piece. Practised on every process piece of the year. Teacher note: a room without devices does the three typed pages in the computer lab or as handwritten pages with a typed final piece later in the unit; the plan names which.

words: plan; draft; revise; edit; feedback; sentence pattern; style; tone
notes: Developing and strengthening writing with some guidance and support from peers and adults by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach (W.6.5), with editing up to and including grade 6 conventions. L.6.3 sits here because revision is where it is practised: varying sentence patterns for meaning, interest and style (L.6.3a, through sentence combining on sentences from the anchor text and the student's draft) and keeping style and tone consistent (L.6.3b). Grade 5 asked for the same process with guidance; grade 6 adds 'trying a new approach' and consistent style and tone. Each process piece has a named feedback step. Limit: revising for clarity and style; revising for how well purpose and audience are served is grade 7.

words: research question; source; credible; quote; paraphrase; plagiarism; bibliography
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-research-contribution (a short research project from several sources)
notes: Conducting short research projects to answer a question from several sources, refocusing the question when the sources call for it (W.6.7), and gathering information from print and digital sources, judging the credibility of each, quoting or paraphrasing without plagiarism, and giving basic bibliographic information (W.6.8). Grade 5 built knowledge from several sources and listed them; grade 6 adds judging credibility, refocusing the inquiry, and basic citation. Two or three short projects a year on the unit's topic, each a few days, from a teacher-checked source set. Limit: basic bibliographic information; search terms, accuracy and a standard citation format are grade 7.

words: analysis; reflection; evidence; response; routine; draft
notes: Drawing evidence from literary and informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research (W.6.9; W.6.9a and b apply the grade 6 reading standards, for example comparing genres or tracing an argument), and writing routinely over both long and short time frames (W.6.10). This is the daily written question on the day's text and the one-sitting evidence paragraph: point, quoted evidence, explanation. Grade 5 drew evidence the same way at grade 5 demand; grade 6 applies it to grade 6 reading standards. Practised on every reading day. Limit: one piece of evidence per point; several pieces per point are grade 7.

words: discussion; prepare; evidence; role; paraphrase; perspective; build on
notes: Taking part in discussions one-on-one, in groups and teacher-led on grade 6 texts and topics: come prepared and cite the text (SL.6.1a), follow agreed rules, set goals and deadlines, take roles (b), ask and answer with elaboration (c), and review key ideas, showing other views through reflection and paraphrase (d). Grade 5 asked the same with less independence; grade 6 adds setting goals and deadlines and paraphrasing several perspectives. A taught routine with sentence frames that fade across the year; a formal text discussion at least every two weeks. Limit: understanding others' views; changing one's own view on new information is grade 7.

words: present; claim; finding; eye contact; volume; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings in a logical order with pertinent facts and details, with eye contact, adequate volume and clear speech (SL.6.4); adding graphics, images or sound to clarify (SL.6.5); and adapting speech to the setting, using formal English when it fits (SL.6.6). Grade 5 reported on a topic in order; grade 6 presents claims and findings and adds adapting register to the context. Two or three short talks a year, each tied to a research project or argument from the unit. Limit: sequencing ideas logically; emphasising salient points in a focused way is grade 7.

words: pronoun; subjective; objective; possessive; intensive; antecedent; shift
notes: Using pronouns correctly in writing and speech: proper case (L.6.1a), intensive pronouns (b), no shifts in pronoun number and person (c), no vague pronouns with unclear antecedents (d), and recognising variations from standard English in one's own and others' writing and speaking, with strategies to improve conventional expression (e). Grade 5 worked on conjunctions and verb tense; grade 6 is the pronoun year. Taught in short openers on sentences from the anchor texts and the student's own drafts, then applied in editing. Teacher note: L.6.1e is taught as choosing the right form for the setting; home language and dialects are respected and never corrected as wrong in themselves.

words: comma; parentheses; dash; nonrestrictive; parenthetical; spell
notes: Using commas, parentheses and dashes to set off nonrestrictive and parenthetical elements (L.6.2a) and spelling correctly (L.6.2b), with spelling of long words taught through word parts. Grade 5 used commas after introductory elements and in a series; grade 6 adds the three ways to set off an extra element and when each fits. Model sentences come from the anchor texts; practised in editing. Limit: setting off elements; commas between coordinate adjectives are grade 7, and dashes and ellipses for a pause or omission are grade 8. Teacher note: the dash is taught because the standard asks for it; how model sentences show it beside the Curio Class house rule against the em dash in its own prose is an open question with the lead.

words: context; root; affix; Greek; Latin; dictionary; verify; cause and effect; part and whole
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 6 reading by choosing among strategies: context (L.6.4a), Greek and Latin affixes and roots (b, for example aud in audience, auditory, audible), print and digital reference works for pronunciation, meaning and part of speech (c), and checking the guess in context or a dictionary (d). L.6.5b sits here: using word relationships (cause and effect, part and whole, item and category) to understand each word. Grade 5 used affixes and roots and reference works; grade 6 adds verifying the first guess and choosing flexibly. Practised on words the unit's texts supply. Limit: common roots; less common roots and specialised references are grade 7.

words: cite; several; evidence; inference; analysis; support
notes: Citing several pieces of textual evidence to support an analysis of what a text says explicitly and what it implies, in literature and literary nonfiction. Grade 6 cited evidence for a point; grade 7 asks for several pieces gathered across the text, so the reader must look beyond the first line that fits. Practised on every anchor of the year, now including longer stories, a short play and longer articles in the middle of the grades 6 to 8 band. RL.7.1 and RI.7.1 share the row because the skill is the same; RI.7.1 adds evidence from data displays. Limit: several pieces; choosing the strongest is grade 8.

words: theme; develop; over the course of; objective summary; shift
notes: Determining a theme and analysing how it develops over the course of a text, and writing an objective summary. Grade 6 found a theme and the details that convey it; grade 7 follows the theme as it grows, turns or deepens from beginning to end (where it is first hinted, where it is tested, where it lands). The summary is now called objective. Practised on original stories of 2,500 to 6,000 words and on the year's long text. Limit: development across the text; its relationship to characters, setting and plot together is grade 8.

words: setting; character; plot; interact; shape; influence; motive
notes: Analysing how particular elements of a story or drama interact, for example how setting shapes characters or plot, or how a character's choice changes the setting. Grade 6 described plot episodes and character change; grade 7 asks how one element acts on another. Practised on original stories where place matters (a flood town, a city summer, a ranch in drought) and the year's short original play. Limit: how elements act on each other; how a single line of dialogue or incident propels the action is grade 8.

words: rhyme; alliteration; repetition; connotation; allusion; tone; stanza
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-greek-myth (mythological allusions met in the grade 7 myth unit)
notes: Determining figurative and connotative meanings and analysing the impact of rhymes and other repeated sounds (alliteration, repetition) on a verse, stanza or section of a story or drama. Grade 6 analysed one word choice's impact on tone; grade 7 adds sound. L.7.5 sits here: L.7.5a interpreting figures of speech including literary, biblical and mythological allusions in context, and L.7.5c connotation (refined, polite, condescending); L.7.5b is owned by e7-word-strategies. Practised on original poems read aloud and silently, and on a few short public-domain poems as paired reads. Limit: sound and word; analogies and allusions as word choice in prose are grade 8.

words: form; soliloquy; sonnet; stage direction; line; meaning; structure
notes: Analysing how a drama's or poem's form or structure contributes to its meaning: what a soliloquy lets the audience hear, how a sonnet's turn changes the argument, how stage directions carry what dialogue does not. Grade 6 analysed how one part fits the whole; grade 7 asks what the form itself does. Practised on an original short play with a soliloquy and on original sonnets and fixed-form poems, with one older public-domain sonnet as a paired read (BASELINE rule 29). Limit: one form at a time; comparing the structures of two texts is grade 8.

words: point of view; narrator; character; contrast; perspective; alternating
notes: Analysing how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators, for example a story told in alternating chapters by two siblings. Grade 6 explained how one narrator's view is built; grade 7 sets two or more views against each other and asks how the author makes the difference. The point-of-view model gains a second column. Practised on original stories with two narrators or with a narrator whose view clashes with another character's, 2,000 to 5,000 words. Limit: contrast among characters; the gap between characters and the reader (dramatic irony) is grade 8.

words: medium; version; technique; lighting; sound; camera angle; delivery
notes: Comparing a written story, drama, poem or nonfiction text with its audio, filmed, staged or multimedia version, analysing the effects of techniques unique to each medium (lighting, sound, colour, camera angle; for a speech, how delivery changes the impact of the words). RL.7.7 and RI.7.7 share the row: the same analysis in literature and in nonfiction. Grade 6 compared the experience of reading and watching; grade 7 names the medium's own techniques and their effects. Practised on a scene of the year's original play recorded for the course, and on a public-domain recorded speech with its transcript. Limit: analysing effects; judging how faithful a production is and the director's choices is grade 8. Teacher note: recordings are made for the course or in the public domain.

words: historical fiction; account; portrayal; period; alter; accurate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-athenian-democracy (a story set in the Athenian assembly read beside a historical account)
notes: Comparing a fictional portrayal of a time, place or character with a historical account of the same period, to understand how fiction writers use or change history. Grade 6 compared texts in different genres on a theme; grade 7 sets fiction against history and asks what the writer kept, invented and changed, and why. Practised on an original historical story with a historical account of the same period: for example a story set in the Athenian assembly with a short account of Athenian democracy (joining the grade 7 social studies year), or a story of a 1930s dust storm with recent public-domain government accounts. Each text 800 to 3,000 words. Limit: one portrayal and one account.

words: stamina; reread; complex; long text; independent reading; log
notes: Reading and understanding literature and literary nonfiction in the grades 6 to 8 complexity band by the end of the year, with support at the high end. The standard's wording does not change from grade 6; the demand climbs through the texts (a working split, ours: grade 7 anchors centred in the middle of the band, more at its top with support) and the volume (one long text read whole, longer anchors, independent reading with a log and conferences). RL.7.10 and RI.7.10 share the row; the year's anchors aim at about 55 percent informational.

words: central idea; develop; objective summary; supporting detail; media; clarify
notes: Determining two or more central ideas in a text and analysing their development over the course of the text, and writing an objective summary. SL.7.2 sits here: analysing the main ideas and details in information presented in diverse media and formats (a narrated graph, a short recorded explainer) and how they clarify the topic. Grade 6 found one central idea and the details that convey it; grade 7 tracks two or more as they develop. Practised on longer informational articles (1,200 to 3,000 words) and chapters of a nonfiction book, plus one media source per unit. Limit: development of the ideas; their relationship to supporting ideas in detail is grade 8.

words: interaction; influence; individual; event; idea; cause
notes: Analysing the interactions between individuals, events and ideas in a text: how an idea moves people to act, or how a person changes the course of events or ideas. Grade 6 followed one individual, event or idea through a text; grade 7 asks how they act on each other. Practised on history and science narratives: a biography chapter of a scientist, an account of how a public health idea spread, 1,000 to 3,000 words. Limit: interactions; the connections and distinctions an author draws through comparisons, analogies and categories are grade 8.

words: word choice; tone; connotation; technical; domain-specific; impact
notes: Determining figurative, connotative and technical meanings in informational text and analysing the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone (an article that calls a plan 'bold' and another that calls it 'reckless'). L.7.6 sits here: the unit's general academic and domain words, drawn from these texts and returned to. Grade 6 determined meanings; grade 7 adds the impact of word choice on tone in nonfiction, as RL.6.4 did in literature. Practised on the unit's informational anchors. Limit: one word choice's impact; analogies and allusions as word choice are grade 8.

words: structure; organise; major section; whole; develop; heading
notes: Analysing the structure an author uses to organise a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas. Grade 6 analysed how one part fits; grade 7 looks at the whole design (why a report goes problem, history, three cases, recommendation). Practised on longer reports and nonfiction chapters with sections, 1,500 to 3,500 words, often recent public-domain government reports. Limit: the major sections; the role of each sentence in a single paragraph is grade 8.

words: position; point of view; purpose; distinguish; others; counter
notes: Determining an author's point of view or purpose and analysing how the author distinguishes their position from that of others ('some argue that...; but the data show...'). Grade 6 explained how one author's view is conveyed; grade 7 adds how the author sets that view apart from others'. Practised on opinion essays and argumentative articles that name another view, original or recent public-domain, 600 to 2,000 words. Limit: distinguishing positions; how an author acknowledges and answers conflicting evidence is grade 8.

words: reasoning; sound; relevant; sufficient; evidence; evaluate
notes: Tracing and evaluating the argument and specific claims in a text, judging whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient. SL.7.3 sits here: the same evaluation of a speaker's argument. Grade 6 sorted supported from unsupported claims; grade 7 asks whether the support is enough and whether the reasoning holds. The argument-map gains a mark for each link (sound or not) and each evidence box (relevant, sufficient). Practised on editorials, public comment letters and recorded speeches, 500 to 1,500 words. Limit: soundness and sufficiency; recognising when irrelevant evidence is brought in is grade 8.

words: emphasise; interpretation; key information; shape; author; topic
notes: Analysing how two or more authors writing on the same topic shape their presentations of key information by stressing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts. Grade 6 compared one author's presentation of events with another's; grade 7 asks how each author's choices of evidence and interpretation shape the reader's understanding. Practised on paired articles on one unit topic (for example two accounts of a city's response to an epidemic), each 600 to 2,000 words. Limit: different emphasis and interpretation; texts that conflict on matters of fact are grade 8.

words: claim; opposing claim; acknowledge; logical; cohesion; credible; accurate
notes: Writing arguments: introduce the claim and acknowledge alternate or opposing claims, organising reasons and evidence logically (W.7.1a); support with logical reasoning and relevant evidence from accurate, credible sources (b); create cohesion among claim, reasons and evidence (c); formal style (d); a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument (e). Grade 6 organised one claim's reasons clearly; grade 7 adds acknowledging opposing claims, logical reasoning and cohesion. Two pieces a year, one through the full process. Limit: acknowledging the other side; distinguishing one's claim from it and handling counterclaims is grade 8.

words: preview; cohesion; transition; definition; classification; precise
notes: Writing informative and explanatory texts: introduce the topic clearly and preview what follows, organising by definition, classification, comparison or cause and effect with headings and graphics (W.7.2a); develop with facts and quotations (b); transitions that create cohesion (c); precise and domain words (d); formal style (e); a conclusion that follows and supports (f). Grade 6 used transitions to clarify; grade 7 adds a preview and cohesion. Two to three pieces a year on the unit's topic. Limit: organising strategies named in the standard; organising into broader categories is grade 8.

words: point of view; narrator; pacing; capture; reflect; conclusion
notes: Writing narratives: establish a context and a point of view and introduce the narrator and characters (W.7.3a); use dialogue, pacing and description (b); transitions for sequence and shifts (c); precise, sensory language that captures the action (d); and a conclusion that reflects on the events (e). Grade 6 introduced a narrator; grade 7 adds establishing a point of view on purpose, capturing action and reflecting in the ending. Model texts are the unit's two-narrator stories. Two pieces a year. Limit: reflection in the conclusion; reflection as a technique inside the narrative is grade 8.

words: task; purpose; audience; link; cite; publish; collaborate
notes: Producing clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience (W.7.4), and using technology to produce and publish writing, linking to and citing sources, and collaborating (W.7.6). Grade 6 published and typed three pages; grade 7 adds linking to and citing sources in published work. Practised on every process piece; one piece a year is published with live links to its sources. Teacher note: a room without devices prints its pieces with a source list in place of links.

words: revise; purpose; audience; concise; wordiness; redundancy; precise
notes: Strengthening writing with some guidance and support by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach, now focusing on how well purpose and audience have been served (W.7.5), with editing up to grade 7 conventions. L.7.3 sits here: choosing language that is precise and concise and cutting wordiness and redundancy (L.7.3a). Grade 6 revised for clarity and consistent style; grade 7 adds revising against purpose and audience and cutting wordiness. Editing applies the grade 6 pronoun work. Each process piece has a named feedback step.

words: search term; accuracy; credibility; citation format; related question; investigate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-research-greek (judging credible and relevant sources in a research task)
notes: Conducting short research projects from several sources and generating further related, focused questions (W.7.7), and gathering information with effective search terms, judging the credibility and accuracy of each source, quoting or paraphrasing without plagiarism, and following a standard citation format (W.7.8). Grade 6 refocused the question, judged credibility and gave basic bibliographic information; grade 7 adds search terms, accuracy, new questions and a standard format. Two or three projects a year on the unit's topic. Limit: questions given or chosen from a list; a self-generated question with several avenues is grade 8.

words: analysis; reflection; evidence; several; response; routine
notes: Drawing evidence from texts for analysis, reflection and research, applying the grade 7 reading standards (W.7.9a, for example fiction against history; W.7.9b, evaluating an argument), and writing routinely over long and short time frames (W.7.10). The daily written question and the one-sitting evidence paragraph now use several pieces of evidence. Grade 6 applied grade 6 reading standards with one piece per point; grade 7 applies grade 7 standards with several. Practised on every reading day.

words: prepare; research; elaborate; on topic; acknowledge; modify; view
notes: Discussions on grade 7 texts and topics: come prepared, having read or researched (SL.7.1a); follow rules, track progress toward goals and deadlines (b); ask questions that draw out elaboration and bring talk back on topic (c); acknowledge new information and, when warranted, change one's own view (d). Grade 6 set goals and paraphrased others; grade 7 adds tracking progress, steering back to the topic and modifying one's view. A formal text discussion at least every two weeks, frames faded further than in grade 6.

words: salient; focused; coherent; emphasise; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings, emphasising salient points in a focused, coherent way with pertinent details and examples (SL.7.4); multimedia and visual displays that clarify claims and emphasise salient points (SL.7.5); adapting speech to context with formal English when it fits (SL.7.6). Grade 6 sequenced ideas logically; grade 7 asks the speaker to choose and stress what matters most. Two or three talks a year tied to research or argument.

words: phrase; clause; simple; compound; complex; compound-complex; modifier; dangling
notes: Explaining what phrases and clauses do in general and in particular sentences (L.7.1a), choosing among simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences to show relationships among ideas (b), and placing phrases and clauses well, fixing misplaced and dangling modifiers (c). Grade 6 varied sentence patterns in revision; grade 7 names the parts and chooses sentence types on purpose. Taught through sentence combining on anchor-text sentences, applied in drafts. Limit: phrases and clauses; verbals and verb voice and mood are grade 8.

words: coordinate adjective; comma; spell
notes: Using a comma between coordinate adjectives (a fascinating, enjoyable film; but not an old green shirt) and spelling correctly (L.7.2a and b). Grade 6 set off nonrestrictive elements; grade 7 adds the test for coordinate adjectives (can the order switch and 'and' go between?). Spelling of long words continues through word parts. Practised in openers and editing.

words: root; affix; specialised; reference; synonym; antonym; analogy; verify
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 7 reading: context (L.7.4a), Greek and Latin roots and affixes (b, for example bell in belligerent, bellicose, rebel), general and specialised reference works (c), and checking the guess (d). L.7.5b sits here: synonym, antonym and analogy relationships to understand each word. Grade 6 used common references; grade 7 adds specialised references and analogy. Practised on words from the unit's texts.

words: strongest; evidence; cite; analysis; inference; weigh
notes: Citing the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what a text says explicitly and what it implies. Grade 7 gathered several pieces; grade 8 asks the reader to weigh them and choose the strongest, saying why it beats the others. Practised on every anchor, now at the high end of the grades 6 to 8 band. RL.8.1 and RI.8.1 share the row; RI.8.1 adds weighing data against testimony.

words: theme; relationship; character; setting; plot; objective summary
notes: Determining a theme and analysing its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to the characters, setting and plot, and writing an objective summary. Grade 7 tracked a theme's development; grade 8 ties that development to what the characters do, where they are and what happens. Practised on original stories and novella chapters of 3,000 to 8,000 words and the year's long text.

words: dialogue; incident; propel; reveal; provoke; decision
notes: Analysing how particular lines of dialogue or incidents propel the action, reveal a character or provoke a decision. Grade 7 analysed how story elements act on each other; grade 8 zooms to the single line or incident that moves the story. Practised on original stories and the year's original play, where a short exchange turns the plot.

words: analogy; allusion; irony; pun; connotation; tone; word choice
notes: Determining figurative and connotative meanings and analysing the impact of word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies and allusions to other texts. L.8.5 sits here: L.8.5a verbal irony and puns in context, L.8.5c connotation (bullheaded, willful, firm, resolute); L.8.5b is owned by e8-word-strategies. Grade 7 added sound; grade 8 adds analogy, allusion and irony. Practised on original stories and poems that allude to texts read in earlier units or grades (a myth, a well-known speech).

words: structure; compare; meaning; style; frame; chronology
notes: Comparing and contrasting the structure of two or more texts and analysing how each structure contributes to its meaning and style (a story told in order against one told in reverse; a poem in free verse against one in a fixed form on the same subject). Grade 7 analysed what one form does; grade 8 sets two structures side by side. Practised on paired original texts on one unit topic, each 500 to 3,000 words.

words: dramatic irony; suspense; humour; audience; reader; point of view
notes: Analysing how differences between what characters know and what the audience or reader knows (dramatic irony) create suspense or humour. Grade 7 contrasted characters' points of view; grade 8 adds the reader as a party to the point-of-view model. Practised on the year's original play and on original mystery and comic stories.

words: production; faithful; depart; director; actor; interpretation; script
notes: Analysing how far a filmed or live production of a story or drama stays faithful to or departs from the text or script, and evaluating the choices the director or actors made. Grade 7 analysed techniques unique to each medium; grade 8 judges the production's choices against the text. Practised on the year's original play, staged by the class in two versions, and on a course-made recording. Teacher note: recordings are made for the course or in the public domain.

words: myth; traditional story; character type; pattern; archetype; rendered new
notes: Analysing how a modern work of fiction draws on themes, patterns of events or character types from myths and traditional stories, and how the material is made new. Grade 7 compared fiction with history; grade 8 compares a modern story with its old source. Practised on an original modern story built on a myth or folktale, with the traditional story (public domain) as the paired read (BASELINE rule 29). Teacher note: the standard names religious works such as the Bible as one possible source ('such as', not required); the pick, open with the lead, is myths and folktales as the sources, with no religious work as an anchor; any religious text used is read as literature and no student is asked to state a belief.

words: independent; high end; complex; long text; stamina; log
notes: Reading and understanding literature and literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6 to 8 band independently and proficiently by the end of the year. Grade 7 read in the band with support at the high end; grade 8 removes the support at the top: the year's later anchors are read without the before-reading help. One long text read whole, longer anchors, independent reading with a log and conferences. RL.8.10 and RI.8.10 share the row; the anchors aim at about 55 percent informational.

words: central idea; supporting idea; develop; objective summary; relationship
notes: Determining a central idea and analysing its development over the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas, and writing an objective summary. Grade 7 tracked two or more central ideas; grade 8 asks how the supporting ideas build, limit or qualify the central one. Practised on long articles, report chapters and essays of 1,500 to 4,000 words.

words: connection; distinction; analogy; comparison; category
notes: Analysing how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas or events, through comparisons, analogies or categories (an explainer that compares the bloodstream to a road network; a history that sorts reformers into groups). Grade 7 analysed interactions; grade 8 asks how the author's comparisons and categories make the links. Practised on science and history explainers and essays, 1,000 to 3,000 words.

words: word choice; analogy; allusion; tone; technical; domain-specific
notes: Determining figurative, connotative and technical meanings in informational text and analysing the impact of word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies and allusions to other texts (a speech that echoes a founding document). L.8.6 sits here: the unit's general academic and domain words from these texts. Grade 7 analysed one word choice's impact; grade 8 adds analogy and allusion in nonfiction. Practised on speeches, essays and articles, recent public-domain or original.

words: paragraph; sentence; role; develop; refine; key concept
notes: Analysing in detail the structure of one paragraph, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept (the sentence that defines, the one that limits, the one that gives the case). Grade 7 analysed how major sections build the whole; grade 8 works at sentence level inside a paragraph. Practised on dense paragraphs from science and history texts and from essays, 100 to 300 words each, reread several times.

words: acknowledge; respond; conflicting; viewpoint; concede; rebut
notes: Determining an author's point of view or purpose and analysing how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints (concede, then rebut; answer an objection with data). Grade 7 analysed how an author distinguishes a position from others; grade 8 asks how the author answers them. Practised on argumentative essays and public letters that take on an objection, original or recent public-domain, 800 to 2,500 words.

words: medium; advantage; disadvantage; motive; commercial; political; purpose
notes: Evaluating the advantages and disadvantages of different mediums (print or digital text, video, multimedia) for a topic or idea (RI.8.7), and analysing the purpose of information presented in diverse media and evaluating the social, commercial or political motives behind it (SL.8.2). Grade 7 analysed each medium's portrayal of a subject; grade 8 judges which medium serves the purpose and why the presenter chose it. Practised on one topic shown in a print article, a short video and an infographic made for the course, and on public notices and advertisements written for the course. Teacher note: no real brand or company appears; advertisements are written for the course.

words: delineate; irrelevant; sound; sufficient; relevant; reasoning
notes: Delineating and evaluating the argument and claims in a text, judging soundness and the relevance and sufficiency of evidence, and recognising when irrelevant evidence is introduced (RI.8.8). SL.8.3 sits here: the same on a speaker's argument. Grade 7 judged soundness and sufficiency; grade 8 adds catching irrelevant evidence. Practised on editorials, public hearing testimony and recorded speeches, 600 to 2,000 words.

words: conflict; fact; interpretation; disagree; source; verify
notes: Analysing a case in which two or more texts give conflicting information on the same topic and identifying where they disagree on matters of fact or of interpretation. Grade 7 analysed how authors stress different evidence; grade 8 sorts real factual conflict from differing interpretation and asks which can be checked. Practised on paired or triple texts on one unit topic (two accounts of a historical event, two reports with different figures), each 500 to 2,000 words.

words: counterclaim; distinguish; rebut; cohesion; logical; credible
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-civic-action (a proposal argued to an audience)
notes: Writing arguments: introduce the claim, acknowledge and distinguish it from alternate or opposing claims, and organise reasons and evidence logically (W.8.1a); logical reasoning and relevant evidence from accurate, credible sources (b); cohesion among claims, counterclaims, reasons and evidence (c); formal style (d); a conclusion that follows and supports (e). Grade 7 acknowledged opposing claims; grade 8 distinguishes the claim from them and works counterclaims into the argument. Two pieces a year, one through the full process.

words: broader category; well-chosen; varied transition; cohesion; preview
notes: Writing informative and explanatory texts: introduce and preview, organising ideas into broader categories with headings and graphics (W.8.2a); develop with relevant, well-chosen facts and quotations (b); varied transitions for cohesion (c); precise and domain words (d); formal style (e); a conclusion that follows and supports (f). Grade 7 used the named strategies and cohesion; grade 8 adds broader categories, well-chosen evidence and varied transitions. Two to three pieces a year on the unit's topic.

words: reflection; relationship; point of view; pacing; time frame
notes: Writing narratives: context and point of view (W.8.3a); dialogue, pacing, description and reflection (b); transitions that show the relationships among experiences and events, not just their order (c); precise, sensory language (d); a conclusion that reflects (e). Grade 7 reflected in the ending; grade 8 makes reflection a technique inside the narrative and links events by meaning. Model texts include the year's modern myth retellings. Two pieces a year, one through the full process.

words: task; purpose; audience; present; efficient; publish
notes: Producing clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience (W.8.4), and using technology to produce and publish writing and present the relationships between information and ideas efficiently, and to collaborate (W.8.6). Grade 7 linked and cited sources; grade 8 adds presenting how ideas relate (a linked page, a diagram, a table) efficiently. Teacher note: without devices, the relationships are shown on paper with a hand-drawn diagram.

words: revise; purpose; audience; active voice; passive voice; mood; effect
notes: Strengthening writing with some guidance and support, focusing on purpose and audience (W.8.5), with editing up to grade 8 conventions. L.8.3 sits here: using active and passive voice and conditional and subjunctive mood for effect (stressing the actor or the action; expressing doubt or a state contrary to fact). The W.8.5 wording is the same as grade 7; the climb is in the conventions edited (grades 6 to 8) and the L.8.3 choices, and in longer pieces. Each process piece has a named feedback step.

words: self-generated question; avenue; search term; accuracy; citation format
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-court-research (a research question answered from court and news sources)
notes: Conducting short research projects to answer a question, including one the student generates, and generating focused questions that open several avenues (W.8.7), with W.8.8 as in grade 7 (search terms, credibility and accuracy, quoting and paraphrasing, a standard citation format). Grade 7 generated related questions; grade 8 adds the student's own question and several avenues of exploration; the W.8.8 wording is unchanged from grade 7 and the climb is in source range and independence. Two or three projects a year, the last a student-chosen question on the unit topic.

words: analysis; reflection; strongest evidence; response; routine
notes: Drawing evidence from texts for analysis, reflection and research, applying grade 8 reading standards (W.8.9a, a modern story and its myth; W.8.9b, delineating an argument), and writing routinely over long and short time frames (W.8.10). The daily written question and the one-sitting evidence paragraph now choose the strongest evidence. Grade 7 used several pieces; grade 8 chooses and defends the best.

words: decision-making; connect; qualify; justify; evidence; several speakers
notes: Discussions on grade 8 texts and topics: come prepared (SL.8.1a); rules for discussion and decision-making, tracking goals and deadlines (b); questions that connect the ideas of several speakers, answering with evidence (c); acknowledging new information and qualifying or justifying one's own view in light of evidence (d). Grade 7 modified views and kept talk on topic; grade 8 adds group decision-making, connecting several speakers and qualifying a view. Student-led formal discussions at least every two weeks, frames mostly gone.

words: valid reasoning; relevant evidence; integrate; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings with salient points in a focused way, relevant evidence, sound valid reasoning and well-chosen details (SL.8.4); integrating multimedia and visual displays to clarify, strengthen claims and add interest (SL.8.5); adapting speech to context (SL.8.6). Grade 7 stressed salient points; grade 8 adds sound reasoning and integrated, not added, media. Two or three talks a year, one a formal argument to an audience beyond the class where possible.

words: verbal; gerund; participle; infinitive; active; passive; mood; subjunctive
notes: Explaining the function of verbals (gerunds, participles, infinitives) in general and in particular sentences (L.8.1a), forming and using active and passive voice (b) and the indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional and subjunctive moods (c), and fixing shifts in voice and mood (d). Grade 7 named phrases and clauses; grade 8 adds verbals (phrases built on verb forms), voice and mood. Taught on anchor sentences and applied in drafts.

words: comma; ellipsis; dash; pause; break; omission; spell
notes: Using a comma, ellipsis or dash to show a pause or break (L.8.2a), an ellipsis to mark an omission in a quotation (b), and spelling correctly (c). Grade 7 used commas between coordinate adjectives; grade 8 adds the pause and the omission, used when quoting evidence. Teacher note: the dash is taught because the standard asks for it; how model sentences show it beside the Curio Class house rule against the em dash in its own prose is an open question with the lead.

words: root; affix; context; reference; verify; word relationship
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 8 reading: context (L.8.4a), Greek and Latin roots and affixes (b, for example cede in precede, recede, secede), general and specialised references (c), and checking the guess (d). L.8.5b sits here: using relationships between words to understand each. The wording barely changes from grade 7; the climb is in the roots and the texts. Practised on words from the unit's texts.
